opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one of the hardest open problems in the field right now.

For a long time in generative modeling, especially image and video generation, we relied on metrics like FID or FVD, or on human preference: does this look good, does it look realistic? For world models aimed at Physical AI, that's not enough. A video can look beautiful and still be physically wrong. Objects pass through each other, liquids behave strangely, or a robot arm grasps something in a way that could never happen. If we train a robot or an autonomous vehicle on that, we're teaching it the wrong lessons.

So I think about evaluation on a few levels.

The first is visual quality and temporal consistency. That's the baseline. The world shouldn't flicker, objects shouldn't change identity, and the scene should stay coherent over time.

The second is physical plausibility. Does the model respect gravity, object permanence, collisions, and basic dynamics? We can build targeted test suites for this: dropping objects, stacking, pouring, pushing. We can also compare against physics simulators or real captured data where we know the ground truth. There's also 3D consistency. If you move the camera, does the geometry stay stable? You can actually reconstruct the scene and check that.

The third, which I think matters most, is controllability and action-conditioning. For Physical AI, a world model isn't just a video generator. It's a simulator of the future given an action. If I tell it the robot moves its gripper left by ten centimeters, does the predicted world reflect exactly that? We need to measure how faithfully the model follows the conditioning signals, whether those are actions, trajectories, or camera poses.

The ultimate test is downstream usefulness. Does the world model actually help you build a better physical AI system? You can use it to generate synthetic training data and see whether the policy trained on it performs better in the real world. You can use it as a policy evaluator: run a robot policy inside the world model, and check whether the success rate in the world model correlates with the success rate in reality. If that correlation is strong, the world model is genuinely useful, because now you can evaluate thousands of policies cheaply instead of running expensive real-world trials.

So my view is that evaluation has to move from "does it look real" to "is it useful and correct for decision-making." We're still early. The community needs better, standardized benchmarks, and I think building those is as important as building the models themselves. You can only improve what you can measure.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes physical plausibility and downstream usefulness, including real-world performance, but does not mention evaluation by solving real problems with domain experts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. This is actually one of the questions I think about the most, because I believe evaluation is where the field is still quite immature.

Let me start with what I think is the wrong way to do it. A lot of people today evaluate world models the same way they evaluate video generation models. They look at visual quality, they run FVD, they ask human raters which clip looks nicer. That is fine if your goal is entertainment. But for Physical AI, the question is not whether the video looks pretty. The question is whether the model understands the physics well enough that a robot or an autonomous vehicle can rely on it. A video can look beautiful and still have a cup passing through a table, or a car that stops in half a meter. Those failures are invisible to aesthetic metrics, and they are exactly the ones that matter.

So I think about evaluation at three levels.

The first level is physical consistency. Does the model obey the basic rules? Object permanence, gravity, contact, momentum, rigid bodies staying rigid, fluids behaving like fluids. You can build targeted test suites for this. You give the model a scene and an action, and you check whether the outcome is physically plausible, often by comparing against a simulator or against real recorded outcomes. These are almost like unit tests for physics. They are not glamorous, but if a model fails them, nothing downstream will work.

The second level is counterfactual and controllability evaluation. A world model is not just a video predictor. It has to respond correctly to actions. If I tell it the robot arm moves left, the arm had better move left, and the consequences had better follow. So we condition on different action sequences from the same starting state and check that the model produces different, and correct, futures. This is where the model really earns the name world model, because prediction without action conditioning is just forecasting.

The third level, and honestly the one I care about most, is downstream task utility. Does using this world model actually make the robot better? You train a policy in the model's imagination, or you use the model to generate synthetic training data, or you use it for planning, and then you measure success rate on real hardware. That is the ground truth. If a model scores well on every benchmark but the policy trained with it does not transfer, the benchmarks are measuring the wrong thing. We have seen this already. Models that look very similar on video metrics can give very different results when you close the loop with a real robot.

There are two more things I would add.

One is the simulation-to-real gap. Because we are generating the data, we can measure how a policy performs when trained on generated data versus real data. That gap is itself a very honest metric of how good the world model is.

The other is that evaluation has to be domain specific. Driving cares about long-horizon temporal consistency and rare events. Manipulation cares about fine contact and deformable objects. Humanoids care about balance and whole-body dynamics. A single universal score is not going to capture that. I would rather see a family of benchmarks that each test something a practitioner actually needs.

If I had to summarize it in one sentence, I would say we should stop asking whether the world model generates good videos and start asking whether it generates good decisions.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes real-hardware task success and domain-specific benchmarks, but does not describe evaluation with domain experts.

r002.rationale: The response does not contrast the range of problems in Physical AI with coding agents’ shared focus on coding or digital tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether a world model helps an agent make better decisions in the physical world. Generating a video that looks realistic is useful, but visual quality alone doesn’t tell us whether the model understands the consequences of an action.

For Physical AI, I would evaluate a few things. First, action conditioning: if a robot takes a different action, does the model predict the right change in the environment? Second, physical consistency: does an object persist when it’s occluded, and do contact and motion behave plausibly? Third, how do errors accumulate over time? A model can make a convincing short prediction and still be unreliable for planning.

But ultimately, I would want a closed-loop evaluation. Give an agent access to the world model, let it use the model to plan or learn, and measure whether it completes real tasks more successfully. Does it need fewer real-world interactions? Can it handle unfamiliar objects or environments? Does it recognize uncertainty before taking a risky action?

So I would use predictive benchmarks as diagnostics, but the strongest evidence would be improvement on downstream physical tasks. The model needs to be useful for acting, and that’s a higher bar than looking convincing.

r001.rationale: It recommends evaluating downstream physical tasks and real-world success, but does not mention solving problems with domain experts or give that approach particular importance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether a world model helps an agent make better decisions in the physical world. Generating a video that looks realistic is useful, but that alone doesn’t tell us whether the model understands the consequences of an action.

For Physical AI, I would evaluate it at a few levels. First, does it predict what happens when you take an action? If a robot pushes an object, does the model predict how that object moves, including contact and interaction with other objects? Second, can you use those predictions for planning? And ultimately, does planning with the model improve the robot’s success rate on real tasks?

You also need to test generalization—new objects, new environments, and situations that weren’t represented in training. And uncertainty matters. The physical world isn’t completely predictable, so a useful model should represent multiple plausible outcomes and recognize when its predictions are unreliable.

So I wouldn’t look for just one score. I’d want a combination of prediction quality, physical consistency, and, most importantly, performance in closed-loop tasks, where the agent acts, observes the result, and adjusts. That’s where you find out whether the world model is actually useful.
